text.p: A rising tide of Israeli-Palestinian violence is fast overtaking peacemaking, as clashes on the West Bank intensify but diplomacy crawls at snail's pace.

Top Palestinian negotiators Saeb Erekat and Mahmoud Abbas set off for Washington on Wednesday for talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and special envoy Dennis Ross on launching an eagerly anticipated U.S. peace initiative.
In Hebron on the West Bank, Palestinian youths armed with stones and petrol bombs took on Israeli troops who responded with tear gas and rubber bullets, wounding 31 Arabs.

Street battles have flared nearly every day since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent bulldozers on March 18 to start work on a Jewish settlement on an East Jerusalem hill called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

"The minute Netanyahu announces a halt to all settlement activities, including in Jabal Abu Ghneim...he would have actually declared his commitment to the peace process," Erekat told Israel television.
Palestinians see the settlement as an attempt to pre-empt future talks on East Jerusalem's status. Israel says it can build where it likes in the city it calls its "eternal" capital.

Netanyahu, back from crisis talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday, said the only path out of the crisis was a PLO crackdown on militants to prevent attacks such as a March 21 Tel Aviv suicide bombing that killed three Israeli women.

"The first principle that President Clinton and I discussed and agreed upon is that there must be an absolute condemnation and battle against terrorism on the Palestinian side because this is the first condition...of peace," Netanyahu told visiting foreign mayors on Wednesday.

PLO officials said Palestinian security chiefs refused a request by U.S. Central Intelligence Agency and Israeli security officials, at a secret meeting attended by President Yasser Arafat in Gaza on Tuesday, to restore security ties with Israel.

"The PLO security chiefs in the West Bank and Gaza Strip who attended the meeting refused to restore security cooperation until political contacts at all levels, including peace talks, were resumed by Israel," one official said.

The Gaza meeting, which state-owned Israel Television's military correspondent said was confirmed by Israeli security officials, came on the same day that three Palestinians were shot dead by Jewish settlers and soldiers in Hebron.
Israel said after the Tel Aviv bombing it would put political talks on hold until the PLO strengthened security cooperation against "terror".

The PLO insists security and political talks must go hand in hand: "Without there being any progress in the political direction there can be no coordination," Palestinian West Bank Preventive Security Chief Jibril Rajoub told Israel Television.
Netanyahu, who on Wednesday set off on a four-day trip to the Netherlands and Italy, saw no quick U.S. fix to the crisis.

"I think that these will be ongoing discussions. I think the United States will talk to the Palestinians, they will talk to us again, talk to the Palestinians again -- it will require a process before we have a result," he said.
In a moment of rare agreement, Palestinian cabinet minister Hanan Ashrawi in Washington echoed Netanyahu's outlook.
"We are discussing in a very candid and thorough and honest way the American role and different ways of trying to extricate and resucitate the process," Ashrawi told CNN.
"Unfortunately there is still nothing clear in the making."
